title: Reflection of Light

notes.heading: 1. Laws of Reflection, Plane Mirror Kinematics & Mirror Rotation
notes.proseLatex: The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in one plane with $\angle i = \angle r$ (single plane-mirror deviation is $\delta = \pi - 2i$; vectorially $\hat{e}_r = \hat{e}_i - 2(\hat{e}_i\cdot\hat{n})\hat{n}$). A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, laterally inverted image at equal perpendicular distance behind the mirror. Rotating the mirror by $\theta$ for a fixed incident ray rotates the reflected ray by $2\theta$, and minimum mirror height to see one's full standing body is $H/2$ (independent of standing distance!).

keyFormulas.label: Plane Mirror Deviation, Rotation & Relative Image Speed
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Solve mirror rotation, image approach speed, and minimum mirror height problems.

examples.problemLatex: An object approaches a stationary plane mirror at $4\text{ m/s}$ while the mirror itself moves toward the object at $1\text{ m/s}$. Find the speed of the image relative to the ground and relative to the object.
stepsLatex: Take rightward $+x$ toward mirror: $v_O = +4$, $v_M = -1$; from $v_I - v_M = -(v_O - v_M)$, $v_I = 2v_M - v_O = 2(-1) - 4 = -6\text{ m/s}$ ($6\text{ m/s}$ ground speed).
Relative speed between object and image $|v_O - v_I| = |4 - (-6)| = 10\text{ m/s}$.

notes.heading: 2. Multiple Images Between Two Inclined Plane Mirrors
notes.proseLatex: For two plane mirrors inclined at angle $\theta$ (in degrees), compute $m = \frac{360^\circ}{\theta}$. If $m$ is an EVEN integer, the number of images is ALWAYS $N = m - 1$ for every object position; if $m$ is an ODD integer, $N = m - 1$ on the angle bisector (symmetric) and $N = m$ off the bisector (asymmetric). Parallel mirrors ($\theta \to 0^\circ$) produce infinitely many images.

keyFormulas.label: Inclined Plane-Mirror Image Count (360° / θ)
keyFormulas.latex: $N = \begin{cases} m - 1, & m\text{ even (any position) or } m\text{ odd (symmetric)}\\ m, & m\text{ odd (asymmetric)}\end{cases}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Count distinct images formed by two mirrors at 90, 60, 72, or 45 degrees.

examples.problemLatex: How many images of a point candle are formed between two perpendicular plane mirrors ($\theta = 90^\circ$)?
stepsLatex: Therefore $N = m - 1 = 3$ images regardless of where the candle is placed.

notes.heading: 3. Concave & Convex Spherical Mirrors (Paraxial Sign Convention)
notes.proseLatex: Under Cartesian sign convention (pole at origin, incident light $+x$), focal length is $f = R/2$ ($f < 0$ for concave, $f > 0$ for convex) and the mirror equation is $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ with transverse magnification $m = -\frac{v}{u} = \frac{f}{f - u}$. Notice a mirror's focal length $f = R/2$ is purely geometric — immersing a mirror in water does NOT change its focal length (unlike lenses!).

keyFormulas.label: Spherical Mirror Equation & Magnification
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Apply Cartesian signs (+/-) to concave and convex mirror image problems.

wbjeebTraps: Walking toward a stationary mirror at speed $v$: your image approaches YOU at $2v$, while its speed relative to the MIRROR is $v$.
Mirror equation has a PLUS sign ($\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$), whereas the lens equation has a MINUS sign ($\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$).
Submerging a concave or convex MIRROR in water leaves its focal length $f = R/2$ completely UNCHANGED!
